newsitem.title: CHINA: China approves two more foreign banks for yuan business.
newsitem.headline: China approves two more foreign banks for yuan business.

text.p: China is opening its domestic banking sector to foreign banks only slowly because it lacks experience in supervising their operations, a senior People's Bank of China official said on Monday.
Di Weiping, executive vice president of the bank's Shanghai branch, said two more of the nine foreign banks so far approved are expected to begin yuan business this week.

Sanwa Bank and Dai-ichi Kangyo Bank would begin before the end of this week with all nine foreign instituions are expected to be doing local loans and deposits by June, he told Reuters in an interview.

But he said there was no timetable for an expansion of the number of foreign banks involved or for easing restrictions, which currently limit the banks to doing yuan business with foreign-funded firms in Shanghai.
"We just started," Di said. "We have no time schedule for authorising more foreign banks to do this business. That will be decided not by us, but by head office.
"We have received several more applications and after preliminary review we have passed some of them on to Beijing with recommendations," he said.

The slowness in opening the domestic banking market to foreign banks is necessary to give the central bank time to build its supervisory framework, and was not related to the competitiveness of the Chinese banks, he said.

"We, the regulators of this market, need to learn how to let the foreign banks integrate with the local currency market. We need to strengthen the supervisory capacity of the central bank, to ensure there is no negative impact as we allow the foreign banks to further integrate with the domestic market," he said.
Di said the internal controls and mechanisms of the foreign banks were different and unfamiliar to the Chinese regulators.
"That doesn't mean that they have less or weaker controls, but they are just different, we need to learn to deal with the difference," he said.
Four of the banks -- Hongkong & Shanghai Banking Corp, the Industrial Bank of Japan, the Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi and Citibank -- have already begun local currency business.
Only foreign banks based in Shanghai have so far been approved to do local currency business, and only if they move their main branch to the Pudong development zone east of Shanghai's city centre.
Di said it was not clear if the central bank head office would approve more banks before year-end, or watch the experiment with the initial nine banks for a longer period.
Expansion of the experiment beyond Shanghai, to Shenzhen and other parts of China, would require approval from the State Council (cabinet), he said.
So far, local currency operations by foreign banks, which began in late March, have gone quite smoothly, Di said.

"They're still in the process of learning. The renminbi (yuan) business is quite different from what they have been conducting, foreign exchange business. These foreign banks are trying to set up control systems, training staff, getting themselves linked into the local interbank market," he said.

Foreign bankers say the main problem they face is sourcing of local currency funds. They are permitted only to take in deposits from foreign-funded firms in Shanghai, or to borrow within strict limits from the interbank market.

"They can also swap funds from their working capital to yuan. At the moment they are doing this to satisfy their fund requirements. But in the longer run if they rely on this, they will face exchange rate risks," Di said.
The main answer, Di said, is for the further development of the interbank market, although current trading volumes on the market are still relatively low and interest rates are high.

" This (the relatively high cost of money on the interbank market) is not only a problem for the foreign banks. The domestic banks are also suffering," he said. "But eventually the cost of the interbank market will come down."
"The authorities will (also) relax the restrictions on deposit taking, so that they can take deposits from, for instance, domestic companies," he added.
He said the interbank market was dominated by the major state banks, who also tended to trade money between themselves directly, not through the interbank market.

"We are encouraging other banks to join in the interbank market. In Shanghai at least, the share of the major banks is coming down," Di said. "The interbank market in Shanghai is already more efficient than in other areas, but this can only be improved very gradually."
